name: Canadian wildfire smoke
rarityNote: Canada's worst fire season on record; nothing in the 2022–2026 record matches this smoke over the US north-east. Draft: verify.

peak.note: Highest 2023-06 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

clues.riddle: Dry thunderstorms lit a forest, and a city to the south turned orange.

questions.prompt: What started most of the fires behind this smoke?
options: Fires spreading north from the United States
Controlled burns that got out of hand
questions.explanation: A cluster of dry thunderstorms on 1 June lit more than 30 fires across western Quebec after an unusually dry spring.
questions.source: NWS Burlington, June 2023 smoke summary: https://weather.gov/media/btv/awareness/firewx/JuneSmoke23.pdf
questions.wrongNote: Most of these fires were lit by dry thunderstorms, not by people.

questions.prompt: Why did New York's sky turn orange in early June 2023?
options: Smoke from wildfires in the US
Industrial smog trapped over the city
Smoke from Quebec carried south on northerly winds
Dust blown in from the Sahara
questions.explanation: More than 150 fires were burning in Quebec on 6 June, and northerly winds carried their smoke hundreds of kilometres south.
questions.source: AP via Fox 10, June 2023: https://www.fox10phoenix.com/news/quebec-evacuations-wildfires-canada
questions.wrongNote: The smoke did not start in the United States.

back: After an unusually dry spring, dry thunderstorms on 1 June lit dozens of fires in Quebec's boreal forest; within a week more than 150 were burning.
Northerly winds pushed the smoke south over Ontario and the US north-east, and on 7 June New York's sky turned orange.
actual: The smoke came from Quebec, hundreds of kilometres north.

name: Indonesian peat haze
rarityNote: The highest September in the 2022–2026 record, 2.4× the 2023 haze year. Draft: compare with 2015 and 2019 before calling it rare.

peak.note: Highest 2026-09 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

clues.riddle: Ground that burns from below fills a strait with smoke.

questions.prompt: Where did Singapore's haze in September 2026 come from?
options: Fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, carried on the wind
Ships in the Strait of Malacca
questions.explanation: Singapore's environment agency detected numerous hotspots across Kalimantan and central and southern Sumatra, where dense smoke had hung since late August.
questions.source: Malay Mail, 4 September 2026: https://www.malaymail.com/news/singapore/2026/09/04/singapore-haze-tips-air-quality-into-unhealthy-range-for-first-time-since-2023/233833
questions.wrongNote: Singapore's own emissions do not change much from month to month; this haze comes and goes with fires elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Why is peat haze so hard to put out?
options: Lightning relights the fires every day
Drained peat smoulders underground, where rain rarely reaches it
questions.explanation: Peat is old, waterlogged plant matter. Drained for plantations it dries out, and once lit it smoulders below the surface for weeks.
questions.source: Page et al., Nature 420, 61–65 (2002), on Indonesia's 1997 peat fires
questions.wrongNote: Rain does reach the surface, but this kind of fire is not burning on the surface.

back: Fires in drained peatland across Kalimantan and southern Sumatra filled the region with smoke from late August. Drained peat dries out and smoulders underground for weeks, so rain rarely puts it out.
Winds carried the smoke to Singapore and Malaysia; on 4 September Singapore's air reached the unhealthy range for the first time since 2023.
actual: The smoke is carried in from fires hundreds of kilometres away.

name: North Indian smog
rarityNote: Every November; 2024 was the worst of the four in the record.

peak.note: Highest 2024-11 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

region: Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and the Gangetic plain

clues.riddle: After the rice harvest, the plain fills with smoke and cold air holds it down.

questions.prompt: What drives most of this month-long November haze?
options: Crop stubble burning plus local pollution, held down by cold still air
questions.explanation: Farm fires in Punjab and Haryana add a large share on peak days: Delhi's Decision Support System put it at 22% on 12 November 2024. The rest is the region's own pollution: traffic, industry, dust and smoke from cooking with wood and dung. Cold, still air holds it all near the ground.
questions.source: Delhi DSS via Outlook Business, November 2024: https://www.outlookbusiness.com/planet/climate/delhi-toxic-smog-crop-burning-surge-air-quality; HEI, State of Global Air 2025, p. 17
questions.wrongNote: Fireworks spike the air for a night or two around Diwali; this haze lasts the whole month.

questions.prompt: In November 2024, where was this haze densest on the Indian side?
options: Over western Bihar, in the eastern Gangetic plain
questions.explanation: In the November 2024 monthly mean the highest cell in this card's area sits in western Bihar, about 700 km east of Delhi. The haze covers the whole plain, not just the capital.
questions.source: CAMS monthly mean as shown in this atlas, PM2.5, November 2024
questions.wrongNote: Delhi gets the headlines, but the haze spans the whole plain.

back: After the rice harvest, farmers in Punjab and Haryana burn the leftover stubble.
Cold, still November air traps that smoke over the plain with the region's traffic, industry, dust and cooking smoke.
actual: Fireworks add a night or two; the month-long smog is crop smoke and local pollution held down by winter air.

helps.text: Cleaner cooking fuel cuts smoke at the source: India's LPG scheme (PMUY) reached over 100 million homes by 2023.
helps.source: HEI, State of Global Air 2025, p. 17

name: Pakistani Punjab smog
rarityNote: Every November; 2024 was the worst of the four in the record, when Lahore's air index passed 1,000.

peak.note: Highest 2024-11 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

region: Lahore, Faisalabad and the Punjab plain

clues.riddle: When the cold comes, a city of gardens disappears into grey air.

questions.prompt: What makes most of Lahore's November smog?
options: Smoke blown in from far away
Local traffic, industry, brick kilns and crop burning, trapped by cold still air
questions.explanation: Studies of Lahore's air point to sources close by. A 2025 national emissions study puts the city's share at 35% transport, 28% heavy industry and 17% brick kilns, and crop burning across the Punjab plain adds smoke in November. Cold, still winter air keeps it all near the ground.
questions.source: Pakistan Air Quality Initiative study via Dawn, December 2025: https://www.dawn.com/news/amp/1960268
questions.wrongNote: Wind can carry smoke across the plain, but most of this smog is made close by.

questions.prompt: In November 2024, where was this haze densest?
questions.explanation: In the November 2024 monthly mean the highest cell sits near Faisalabad, about 110 km west of Lahore. The smog covers the whole plain, not just the big city.
questions.source: CAMS monthly mean as shown in this atlas, PM2.5, November 2024
questions.wrongNote: The big city gets the headlines, but the haze spans the plain.

back: After the rice harvest, farmers across the Punjab plain burn the stubble, while brick kilns, traffic and industry run all winter.
In November 2024 cold, still air held the smoke down until Lahore closed its schools and parks.
actual: Most of it is made on the plain itself and held down by winter air.

name: South American fire smoke
rarityNote: Bolivia's worst fire year on record; September 2024 is more than 3× the average of the other Septembers in the record.

peak.note: Highest 2024-09 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

clues.riddle: In a record drought, forest cleared with fire burns out of control and a continent turns brown.

questions.prompt: What lit most of these fires?
options: People clearing forest and pasture with fire, in a record drought
questions.explanation: Farmers and ranchers clear land with fire every dry season. In 2024 a record drought let those fires spread: in Bolivia they burned over 10 million hectares, mostly in Santa Cruz and Beni, and the government declared a national disaster on 30 September.
questions.source: Reuters via Fiji Times, 2024: https://www.fijitimes.com.fj/bolivia-wildfires-burn-record-area-scorching-homes-and-farms/; IFRC final report MDRBO017
questions.wrongNote: These fires are set by people; the drought let them spread.

questions.prompt: How far did the smoke reach?
options: As far as São Paulo, nearly 2,000 km away
questions.explanation: Smoke spread over Brasília and São Paulo in August and early September, grounding flights and closing schools.
questions.source: NASA Earth Observatory, Smoke fills South American skies, 2024: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/smoke-fills-south-american-skies-153295/
questions.wrongNote: The smoke travelled far beyond the fires.

back: Fires set to clear forest and pasture ran out of control in a record drought across eastern Bolivia and the southern Brazilian Amazon.
By September their smoke covered much of the continent, as far as São Paulo.
actual: People set the fires; a record drought let them spread.

name: Manitoba and Saskatchewan fires
rarityNote: Big Canadian fire seasons come every few years; in this card's area June 2025 is the highest June in the record, ahead of 2023.

peak.note: Highest 2025-06 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

region: Manitoba, Saskatchewan and the northern US plains

clues.riddle: A mining town on a provincial border empties as the forest burns toward it.

questions.prompt: Where did the smoke over North Dakota and Minnesota come from in early June 2025?
options: Fires in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, carried south
questions.explanation: More than 25,000 people were evacuated in three provinces as fires burned across Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Their smoke drifted south, and on 1 June the air in North Dakota and parts of Minnesota reached unhealthy levels.
questions.source: AP via PBS NewsHour, 1 June 2025: https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/thousands-evacuate-as-canadian-wildfires-spread-impacting-air-quality-in-some-u-s-states
questions.wrongNote: This smoke started north of the border.

questions.prompt: Which town of more than 5,000 people was evacuated as a fire crossed from Saskatchewan into Manitoba?
questions.explanation: The fire started near Creighton, Saskatchewan, and crossed into Manitoba; more than 5,000 people left Flin Flon, about 645 km north-west of Winnipeg.
questions.source: AP via PBS NewsHour, 1 June 2025: https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/thousands-evacuate-as-canadian-wildfires-spread-impacting-air-quality-in-some-u-s-states
questions.wrongNote: It was a smaller mining town further north.

back: Fires in the boreal forest of Manitoba and Saskatchewan forced more than 25,000 people from their homes in late May and early June.
Their smoke drifted south over the northern US plains.
actual: The smoke came from Canadian forest fires to the north.

name: Siberian taiga fires
rarityNote: Big Siberian fire summers come every few years; July 2024 is more than 4× any other July in the record.

peak.note: Highest 2024-07 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

clues.riddle: Far from any city, the larch forest burns all summer and the smoke drifts over empty land.

questions.prompt: What started most of these fires, according to officials?
options: People: careless use of fire and illegal grass burning
questions.explanation: Officials blamed most fires on human negligence, including the popular and illegal practice of burning dry grass; heat and dry weather let them spread. By early July more than 100 fires covered about 350,000 hectares in Yakutia alone.
questions.source: Interfax, 2 July 2024: https://interfax.com/newsroom/top-stories/103903/; Reuters via SRN News, July 2024
questions.wrongNote: Lightning starts some, but officials blamed people for most.

questions.prompt: In July 2024, where was this smoke densest?
options: North-east of Lake Baikal, in Zabaykalsky
questions.explanation: In the July 2024 monthly mean the highest cell sits in northern Zabaykalsky, north-east of Lake Baikal, where a state of emergency was also in force.
questions.source: CAMS monthly mean as shown in this atlas, PM2.5, July 2024; Reuters via SRN News, July 2024
questions.wrongNote: Look east of Lake Baikal.

back: In July 2024 more than 100 fires burned in the larch forest of Yakutia, and states of emergency were declared there and in Zabaykalsky.
Smoke over the taiga was more than four times any other July in this record.
actual: Officials blamed most fires on people burning grass and careless use of fire.

name: Saharan dust over Greece
rarityNote: Greece's worst dust episode since 2018; April 2024 is about twice any other April in the record.

peak.note: Highest 2024-04 monthly-mean dust cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

clues.riddle: Southern winds turn an ancient city's sky orange for an evening.

questions.prompt: Why did the sky over Athens turn orange on 23 April 2024?
options: Dust carried from North Africa on southerly winds
questions.explanation: Low pressure over the Mediterranean drove southerly winds that carried Saharan dust from Libya across the sea. Officials called it one of the worst such episodes since 2018.
questions.source: AP via KSAT, 23 April 2024: https://www.ksat.com/news/weird-news/2024/04/23/martian-skies-over-athens-greeces-capital-turns-an-orange-hue-with-dust-clouds-from-north-africa/; BBC via RNZ, April 2024
questions.wrongNote: Orange skies in Greece usually mean fire; this time it was desert dust.

questions.prompt: Athens turned orange, so why is this card's × WHO below 1?
options: The worst dust lasted a few days, and a monthly mean spreads it over the month
WHO has no guideline for dust
The dust never reached the ground
questions.explanation: A monthly mean averages a few dusty days with many clean ones. The month as a whole stays under WHO's daily PM10 guideline, though single days were far above it.
questions.source: WHO 2021 air quality guidelines; CAMS monthly mean as shown in this atlas, PM10, April 2024
questions.wrongNote: Think about how long the episode lasted.

back: On 23 April 2024 southerly winds carried Saharan dust from Libya across the Mediterranean, and the sky over Athens turned orange.
Next morning the Acropolis was hidden from view.
actual: It was desert dust, carried across the sea from Libya.

name: Spanish and Portuguese fires
rarityNote: Spain's worst fire season since 1994; August 2025 is about twice any other August in the record.

peak.note: Highest 2025-08 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

region: Galicia, León, Zamora and northern Portugal

clues.riddle: In a heatwave, the hills between Galicia and León burn faster than crews can reach them.

questions.prompt: What let these fires grow so large?
options: A heatwave with low humidity and strong winds, and fires started by people
questions.explanation: Heat, low humidity and strong wind drove the fires, and many were started by people: police arrested 31 people and investigated 92 more. The Larouco fire in Ourense became the largest in Galicia's recorded history.
questions.source: The Local, 18 August 2025: https://www.thelocal.es/20250818/spains-2025-wildfires-confirmed-as-most-destructive-in-countrys-history; Euronews, 21 August 2025
questions.wrongNote: Lightning starts some fires, but these spread because of heat, wind and people.

questions.prompt: How much land had burned in Spain by late August 2025?
questions.explanation: By 21 August EFFIS satellite data showed about 382,000 hectares burned in Spain in 2025, the most since 1994 and about nine times 2024's total.
questions.source: EFFIS via Euronews, 21 August 2025: https://www.euronews.com/green/2025/08/21/spains-sees-worst-wildfire-season-since-1994-with-382000-hectares-burned-so-far-in-2025
questions.wrongNote: It was the worst season in three decades.

back: In mid-August 2025 a heatwave fed dozens of fires across Galicia, Castilla y León and northern Portugal.
Spain had its worst season since 1994; Portugal had its largest single fire on record.
actual: Heat and wind spread fires, many of them started by people.

name: Harmattan dust
rarityNote: Every dry season (December to March); January 2024 was the dustiest January in the record.

peak.note: Highest 2024-01 monthly-mean dust cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

region: Niger, Nigeria, Chad and the Sahel

clues.riddle: A dry wind from the desert hides the sun over West African cities for weeks.

questions.prompt: Where does most of this dust come from?
options: The Bodélé Depression, a dry lake bed in Chad
questions.explanation: The Bodélé Depression in northern Chad, a dried-up lake bed, is one of the largest dust sources on Earth: nearby mountains funnel strong winds across it, and the Harmattan carries the dust south-west over the Sahel and Nigeria.
questions.source: NASA Earth Observatory, Choking on Saharan dust: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/choking-on-saharan-dust-144970/; Schwanghart and Schütt, Geomorphology 2008
questions.wrongNote: This haze is mostly desert dust, not smoke.

questions.prompt: Why do West African airports see delays in the Harmattan season?
options: Dust cuts visibility below what planes need
questions.explanation: Many West African airports need 800 to 1,200 m of visibility; in Harmattan dust it can fall below 500 m for days, causing delays, diversions and cancellations.
questions.source: Ajayi, West African dust, AfricanSWIFT: https://africanswift.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/84/2020/01/VOAjayi_WestAfricanDust.pdf
questions.wrongNote: Think about what pilots need to see.

back: From December to March the Harmattan blows from the Sahara toward the Gulf of Guinea, carrying dust from the Bodélé Depression in Chad.
In January 2024 the dust over northern Nigeria was the densest in this record.
actual: It is mostly desert dust, carried from Chad on the dry-season wind.

name: Central African savanna fires

peak.note: Highest 2024-12 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

region: Central African Republic, South Sudan and northern DR Congo

clues.riddle: North of the equator the dry season comes, and the grass is burned to make way for new growth.

questions.prompt: Why does this savanna burn every December?
options: People burn grass to clear fields and renew pasture
questions.explanation: In Africa's savannas people set fires for months each dry season, mostly to clear land and manage pasture and cropland. Burning in northern sub-Saharan Africa accounts for about a fifth to a quarter of the world's carbon emissions from fires.
questions.source: NASA Earth Observatory, Fires in Angola: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/fires-in-angola-18655/; Ichoku et al., Environmental Research Letters 2016
questions.wrongNote: Very few of these fires are natural.

questions.prompt: When does the savanna south of the equator burn?
options: From about May to October, its own dry season
questions.explanation: The fire belt follows the dry season: north of the equator it burns from about November to February, south of it from about May to October.
questions.source: NASA Earth Observatory, Fires in Angola: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/fires-in-angola-18655/
questions.wrongNote: The dry season flips across the equator.

back: North of the equator the dry season runs from November to February, and people burn the savanna grass to clear fields and renew pasture.
Africa has about 70% of the world's burned area.
actual: People set most of these fires to manage land.

name: Saharan dust over the Caribbean
rarityNote: Every summer (June to August); June 2025 was the dustiest June in the record.

peak.note: Highest 2025-06 monthly-mean dust cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

region: The Antilles, Hispaniola and the Gulf of Mexico

clues.riddle: A desert's dust crosses an ocean and turns island sunsets hazy.

questions.prompt: Where does this June haze over the Caribbean come from?
options: Smoke and pollution from the islands' cities
Dust from the Sahara, carried across the Atlantic
questions.explanation: Dry, dusty air forms over the Sahara and crosses the Atlantic every three to five days from late spring to early autumn, peaking from late June to mid-August, in a layer about 3 km thick.
questions.source: NOAA via NBC Washington, June 2020: https://www.nbcwashington.com/news/national-international/sahara-dust-blankets-caribbean-air-quality-hazardous/2340444/
questions.wrongNote: This haze is not made in the Caribbean.

questions.prompt: How much Saharan dust falls on the Amazon each year?
questions.explanation: NASA's CALIPSO satellite traced about 182 million tonnes of dust leaving the Sahara each year; 27.7 million tonnes fall on the Amazon basin, bringing phosphorus that the rainforest's soils lose to rain.
questions.source: NASA, February 2015 (Yu et al., Geophysical Research Letters 2015): https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4273/
questions.wrongNote: Much more than you might think.

back: Every summer, dust from the Sahara rides the trade winds across the Atlantic in a dry layer about 3 km thick.
It hazes the sky from the Antilles to the Gulf of Mexico, thousands of kilometres from where it rose.
actual: The dust is carried across the Atlantic from the Sahara.

name: Angolan and Congolese savanna fires
rarityNote: Every dry season (May to October); July 2026 was the smokiest July in the record.

peak.note: Highest 2026-07 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

region: Angola, southern DR Congo and Zambia

clues.riddle: South of the equator, the dry season sets thousands of small fires across the grass.

questions.prompt: What are most of these fires?
options: Many small fires set to clear land and manage pasture and crops
questions.explanation: On 22 August 2019 Angola showed more fire detections than anywhere else on Earth, but NASA noted their low intensity: mostly small farm fires, not large forest fires. People set them for months each year to clear land and manage pasture and cropland.
questions.source: NASA Earth Observatory, Fires in Angola: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/fires-in-angola-18655/; NASA, August 2019
questions.wrongNote: Count the fires, but look at their size.

questions.prompt: In which month does Angola's burning season usually start?
questions.explanation: Burning often begins in May, spreads through the middle of the year and tapers off in September or October.
questions.source: NASA Earth Observatory, Fires in Angola: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/fires-in-angola-18655/
questions.wrongNote: It starts as the rains end.

back: South of the equator the dry season runs from May to October, and people burn grass and fields across Angola, Zambia and southern Congo.
Each fire is small, but thousands burn at once.
actual: Mostly small fires set to manage farmland and pasture.

name: Mainland Southeast Asian burning season

peak.note: Highest 2025-03 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

region: Northern Thailand, Laos and Myanmar's Shan State

clues.riddle: Before the rains, hill fields are burned and a northern Thai city tops the world's pollution charts.

questions.prompt: What drives much of this haze?
options: Burning maize stubble and forest, across three countries
questions.explanation: Farmers burn maize stubble before planting, and forest fires add more. A Chiang Mai University study found the burned share of maize fields across northern Thailand, northern Laos and Shan State rose from 15% in 2015 to 24% in 2019.
questions.source: RFA, September 2023: https://www.rfa.org/english/news/environment/maize-pollution-09122023061657.html; Charoenpanyanet, Chiang Mai University
questions.wrongNote: City traffic adds some, but this haze comes from the fields.

questions.prompt: In April 2023, which city did IQAir rank the world's most polluted major city?
questions.explanation: In April 2023 Chiang Mai topped IQAir's ranking, with PM2.5 more than 66 times the WHO annual guideline.
questions.source: IQAir, Seasonal crop burning pollutes Thailand's skies: https://www.iqair.com/th-en/newsroom/seasonal-crop-burning-pollutes-thailands-skies
questions.wrongNote: It was not one of the usual names.

back: From January to April, farmers in northern Thailand, Laos and Myanmar's Shan State burn maize stubble and forest edges before the rains.
Much of that maize feeds Thailand's livestock.
actual: The smoke comes from burning fields and forest in the hills of three countries.

name: Mexican burning season
rarityNote: Every April and May; 2024 was Mexico's worst fire year since records began in 1998.

peak.note: Highest 2024-05 monthly-mean pm2_5 cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

clues.riddle: Fields are cleared with fire before the rains, and in a hot dry year the flames reach the forest.

questions.prompt: What started many of Mexico's spring 2024 forest fires?
options: Farm burning that got out of control
questions.explanation: Nearly all of Mexico's forest fires are started by people. From January to May 2024, 34.7% came from farm burning that got out of control; 2024 burned more than 1.6 million hectares, the most since records began in 1998.
questions.source: Sader via The Food Tech, 2024: https://thefoodtech.com/industria-alimentaria-hoy/quemas-agricolas-no-controladas-provocan-un-tercio-de-los-incendios-forestales-en-mexico; CONAFOR, 2024
questions.wrongNote: Lightning starts very few of these fires.

questions.prompt: When does Mexico's fire season usually peak?
questions.explanation: Fire season ramps up in February and peaks from mid-March through May, before the rains.
questions.source: NASA Earth Observatory, Fire in southern Mexico, 2024: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/fire-in-southern-mexico-152628/
questions.wrongNote: It comes before the rains.

back: Before the rains, farmers clear fields with fire across southern Mexico and Central America.
In the hot, dry spring of 2024 many burns escaped into forest; Mexico had its largest burned area since records began in 1998.
actual: Nearly all are started by people, about a third by farm burns that escape.

name: Gobi spring dust
rarityNote: Every spring; April 2025 was the dustiest April in the record.

peak.note: Highest 2025-04 monthly-mean dust cell in the footprint, CAMS via Open-Meteo.

areaKm2.note: Footprint cells at or above twice their own median over the record.

reachKm.note: Greatest distance from the source point to such a cell.

region: Inner Mongolia, Gansu and northern China

clues.riddle: Spring storms lift a desert into the air and turn a capital's sky yellow.

questions.prompt: What lifts most of this dust?
options: Spring storms over the Gobi Desert in Mongolia and Inner Mongolia
questions.explanation: Mongolian cyclones, storms that form east of the Altai mountains, drive about a third to a half of the Gobi's dust emissions and most of its worst dust storms. In spring 2023 Mongolia supplied about 42% of the dust over China.
questions.source: Mu and Fiedler, Kiel University, 2025: https://macau.uni-kiel.de/receive/macau_mods_00005691; Advances in Atmospheric Sciences via PreventionWeb, 2023
questions.wrongNote: Cities add their own dust, but these storms start in the desert.

questions.prompt: In April 2025, where was this dust densest?
options: Over western Inner Mongolia, near the Mongolian border
questions.explanation: In the April 2025 monthly mean the highest cell sits in western Inner Mongolia, about 1,300 km west of Beijing, close to where the dust is lifted.
questions.source: CAMS monthly mean as shown in this atlas, dust, April 2025
questions.wrongNote: Look near where the dust is lifted.

back: In spring, cold fronts and cyclones sweep across the Gobi and lift dust from bare, dry ground in Mongolia and Inner Mongolia.
Overgrazing and drought leave more ground bare: about three quarters of Mongolia's land is degraded.
actual: Desert dust lifted by spring storms.
